notes: Quantitative spine for the privacy study: how fast data privacy law spread (Greenleaf's global count, UNCTAD, US states), what notice-and-consent costs people (McDonald & Cranor; Obar & Oeldorf-Hirsch; Amos et al.; Pew 2019/2023), how consent pop-ups actually behave after the GDPR (Degeling et al.; Nouwens et al.), the scale of tracking and data brokerage (Englehardt & Narayanan; ICCL on real-time bidding; FTC 2014; California's data broker registry), enforcement (DLA Piper and CMS GDPR fine totals; California's Sephora/GPC settlement) and the AI-chatbot base on which agents are built (Pew 2025; NBER/OpenAI 2025). Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check in a final audit (95 unique source-quote pairs; all FOUND except the three Obar & Oeldorf-Hirsch quotes, which come from a JSON API and were verified against the decoded abstract instead — see their notes). SSRN, AustLII, unctad.org and idtheftcenter.org block scripted access (HTTP 403 / Cloudflare), so Greenleaf abstracts and UNCTAD pages were read from Internet Archive captures, cited by their archive URL. Derived figures are labelled: UNCTAD 2026 share (computed from UNCTAD's data file, PENDING), California registry counts (rows in CalPrivacy's CSVs), and GDPR cumulative fines for 2022-2024 (back-calculated from DLA Piper totals, estimate=true). Known gaps: (1) Identity Theft Resource Center annual data-compromise counts (series us-data-compromises) could not be built — idtheftcenter.org returns 403 to scripts and the Internet Archive connection kept resetting during this session; (2) Do Not Track adoption and Apple App Tracking Transparency opt-in rates — Flurry publishes its ATT rates only as chart images, and no primary DNT adoption figure was reachable; (3) Global Privacy Control has no published user-count figure; only its legal status (Sephora settlement) is recorded; (4) Greenleaf's 2025 year-by-year list (SSRN 5189972) was not retrievable, so the pre-2011 points are running sums of his 2011 decade counts and no year between editions is interpolated; (5) the popular '76 work days a year to read privacy policies' figure (The Atlantic, 2012) could not be fetched to check how it was derived from McDonald & Cranor, whose own point estimate is 244 hours a year. Web search quota for the session was exhausted mid-slice, which limited the search for alternatives.

myths.claim: People don't really care about privacy — they happily trade their data for free services.
myths.correction: Behaviour and attitudes diverge, but not because people are indifferent. In Pew's 2019 survey 81% of Americans said the risks of company data collection outweigh the benefits; in 2023, 81% were concerned about how companies use their data and 72% wanted more regulation. What people report lacking is control and understanding (see the Pew series on control and understanding in this file), which makes 'agree' a resigned click rather than a considered trade.

myths.claim: Data protection law is a European invention that the rest of the world has not adopted.
myths.correction: Europe started it — Sweden passed the first national data privacy law in 1973 — but lost its majority a decade ago: by January 2015, 56 of 109 national data privacy laws were outside Europe, with Africa the fastest-growing region in the preceding 18 months, and by March 2025 Graham Greenleaf counted 172 countries with such laws.

sources.quote: For the first time, a majority of fifty-six data privacy laws are outside Europe, over 51% of the total. During this eighteen month period, the fastest ‘growth area’ has been Africa.
sources.note: i.e. 56 of the 109 laws counted in January 2015 were outside Europe.

myths.claim: The United States has no consumer privacy law.
myths.correction: There is still no comprehensive federal consumer privacy law, but by 8 September 2026, 23 states had signed comprehensive consumer privacy laws by the IAPP's count, starting with California in 2018. After a year with no new state law in 2025, four more followed in 2026 (Oklahoma, Alabama, Louisiana, Vermont).

myths.claim: Clicking 'accept' on a consent pop-up is a free, informed choice.
myths.correction: When Nouwens and colleagues scraped the five most popular consent platforms on the top 10,000 UK sites in 2019, only 11.8% met three minimal requirements of EU law (explicit consent, reject as easy as accept, no pre-ticked boxes); half had no 'reject all' button, and removing the opt-out from the first page raised consent by 22-23 points in their experiment. Design, not preference, drives much of the 'yes'.

myths.claim: If you clear your cookies, websites can no longer track you.
myths.correction: Tracking also works without stored identifiers. Englehardt and Narayanan's January 2016 crawl of the top million sites found canvas fingerprinting — which identifies a browser from how it draws hidden graphics — on 14,371 sites, 98.2% of it from third-party scripts.

myths.claim: The GDPR is toothless: regulators never fine anyone.
myths.correction: Fines are real and large — about EUR 7.1 billion from 25 May 2018 to 10 January 2026 by DLA Piper's count, including a single EUR 1.2 billion fine on Meta in 2023 — but they are concentrated on a few big-tech firms and a few regulators (Ireland alone accounts for about EUR 4.04 billion), and totals differ by method (CMS counts about EUR 6.11 billion of publicly known fines to 1 March 2026). The fair criticism is uneven, slow enforcement, not absence of enforcement.
